entities.name: Khmer Empire
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Khmer Empire (802–1431 CE) was the largest empire in Southeast Asian history, centered on the hydraulic civilization of Angkor in present-day Cambodia. At its height under Suryavarman II and Jayavarman VII, it controlled modern Cambodia, Thailand, Laos, and southern Vietnam, and built the largest religious monument complex in the world at Angkor Wat.

Angkor Wat, built by Suryavarman II between 1113 and 1150 CE, is the world's largest religious monument — a stone temple mountain symbolizing Mount Meru, the cosmic center of Hindu cosmology. With perimeter walls enclosing over 400 acres and bas-reliefs covering 1,200 meters, it represents the apex of Khmer art and engineering. The broader Angkor complex encompassed over 1,000 temples within an urban area of 400 square kilometers — making it arguably the world's largest pre-industrial city.

The empire's hydraulic engineering — a massive system of reservoirs (barays), canals, and moats — enabled intensive rice cultivation supporting a population estimated at 750,000 to 1 million in Angkor alone. Jayavarman VII (r.1181-1218) converted to Mahayana Buddhism, building Angkor Thom with its face-tower Bayon and 102 hospitals across the empire. Thai Ayutthaya attacks in the 14th-15th centuries and possible hydraulic system failure contributed to Angkor's abandonment around 1431.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Khmer Empire built Angkor Wat and sustained the world's largest pre-industrial city through hydraulic engineering, creating Southeast Asia's greatest civilization and a cultural heritage that defines Cambodian identity.
